query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In these corrosion‐resistant steels, the ability to develop and continually repair a thin, stable Cr2O3 passive film is enhanced by a high density of grain boundaries that serve as rapid diffusion pathways for Cr. This microstructural feature boosts the replenishment of Cr at the surface to offset film loss in aggressive chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional stainless or duplex steel alloy containing sufficient Cr (e.g., ≥12 wt.%) with a coarse‐grained baseline microstructure achieved by standard casting and heat treatment.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermomechanical processing treatment (such as severe plastic deformation followed by appropriate annealing) to refine the grain size, thereby increasing the grain boundary density without changing the bulk chemical composition.
generation.conditions: Expose both the baseline coarse-grained and the refined (fine-grained) steels to controlled corrosive environments representative of chemical-processing applications (for example, immersion in 0.6 M NaCl or mildly acidic aqueous solutions at moderate temperatures) and nuclear-power conditions (elevated temperatures and pressure in simulated reactor coolant water). Testing durations should span sufficient time (tens to hundreds of hours) to observe passive film stabilization or degradation.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased grain boundary density in the fine-grained microstructure, which acts as rapid channels for the diffusion of Cr atoms from the bulk to the surface, thereby supporting the formation and repair of a protective Cr2O3 passive film.
generation.mechanism: Under corrosive conditions, Cr in the steel oxidizes preferentially to form a thin Cr2O3 film. In a fine-grained microstructure, the high density of grain boundaries accelerates the diffusion of Cr, ensuring that any film disruption is rapidly repaired. This self-healing process maintains low dissolution rates of the base metal, conferring superior corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coarse-grained steel, the fine-grained steel will develop a thicker, more uniform and stable Cr2O3 passive film. This will manifest in lower corrosion current densities (via potentiodynamic polarization) and higher impedance values (via EIS), indicating slower corrosion rates.
generation.baseline: Standard, coarse-grained stainless or duplex steel produced by conventional casting and heat treatment, showing typical passivation behavior under similar conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold in steels with adequate Cr content and in environments where the passive film is primarily responsible for corrosion resistance—namely, moderately aggressive chloride-containing or acidic aqueous solutions and within the temperature/pressure regimes encountered in chemical-processing and nuclear coolant systems. It may not apply if other degradation mechanisms (e.g., stress corrosion cracking under high mechanical loads or irradiation effects) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative increase in passive film repair rate and corrosion rate reduction as a function of grain size remains to be determined, and interactions with additional alloying elements (such as Mo or Mn) may also influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of steel samples of identical chemical composition: one with a coarse-grained microstructure (conventional processing) and one with a fine-grained microstructure (obtained via severe plastic deformation and controlled annealing). Subject both sets to identical corrosive conditions (e.g., immersion in 0.6 M NaCl solution at an elevated temperature representative of service environments) for a defined duration. Characterize the passive film using techniques such as X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and electron microscopy, and assess their corrosion behavior using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and potentiodynamic polarization.
measurements: Passive film composition and thickness (via XPS/SEM)
Corrosion current density and impedance (via electrochemical testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fine-grained samples do not exhibit a significantly enhanced Cr2O3 passivation layer—evidenced by comparable (or inferior) film thickness, composition, and corrosion resistance metrics (higher corrosion current or lower impedance) relative to the coarse-grained baseline—then the role of grain-boundary–assisted Cr diffusion in the corrosion mechanism is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Early research reported that stainless steel, Fe-Cr alloy, and CrFe15Ni15 alloy have excellent corrosion resistance due to the dense Cr2O3 passivation film formed on the surface [,,]. Similarly, it was speculated that the Cr2O3 passivation film has the same effect in the corrosion resistance of HEAs. AlCoCrFeNi [], AlxCrFe1.5MnNi0.5 [], and Al0.5CoCrCuFeNiBx [] verified the foregoing speculation. Therefore, for the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating passivation film of this study, it can be obtained from the results of XPS that the Cr2O3 in the passivation film provides good corrosion resistance for the coating, and the addition of trace amount of Nb results in forming a stable metal oxide of Nb2O5 in the passivation film of the coating, which also plays a positive role in the corrosion resistance [,].

cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Cr depletion depth increased significantly in DS2205 compared to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, with an increase in temperature from 450 °C to 650 °C. At 650 °C, the Cr depletion depth for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~50 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~300 μm. This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205. Redox control technique has been utilized for corrosion mitigation in molten fluoride and chloride salts []. Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl3 and CrCl2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. At the redox potential, Co, Ni, and Fe become relatively nobler and their dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable. These findings suggest that Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [].
